title: The Three Little Pigs
strapline: Straw, sticks or bricks? Build a house the wolf can't blow down.
intent: A story children already half-know becomes theirs to retell, in their own words, with their own hands.
Testing straw against sticks against bricks is real science — which materials are strong, which blow away, and why.
The repeated 'I'll huff and I'll puff' gives every child a line to join in with, building confidence with language and story rhythm.
Deciding who is safe, who is scared and who is being unkind stretches early feelings talk and a first sense of fairness.
The tale is a stage for building, hiding, chasing and rescuing — a small world that keeps generating new play.
implementation: Set out three pigs, a wolf and three heaps of building materials — real straw, twigs and toy bricks — so children build and test the houses themselves.
Read or tell the story first with props, then step back and let children run it their own way, however far it wanders.
Model the wonder aloud: 'I wonder which house will keep the little pig safe — shall we blow and find out?'
Bring the huffing and puffing to life — everyone blows, and see whose house really moves; a hairdryer or fan makes it visible.
Feed in strength words as you play: sturdy, wobbly, strong, weak, safe — and ask children to predict before they test.
Follow the children — some will want to build the strongest house ever, others will want the wolf to be sorry and make friends.
key_questions: Which house do you think the wolf can blow down — how could we check?
What makes the brick house so much stronger than the straw one?
How is the little pig feeling now — what does he need?
What could the pigs do so nobody gets frightened?
Can you say the wolf's part with me?

impact.text: Children retell the story loosely with props and join in the repeated refrains.
Children build and test houses, discovering which materials are strong and which blow away.
Children predict what will happen before they blow, and talk about what they found.
Children talk about how the characters feel and what would keep everyone safe.
Children invent their own turns in the story and keep the play going with others.

enhancements: A materials-testing tray — straw, sticks and bricks with a fan or hairdryer for the huffing and puffing.
Junk-modelling to build a wolf-proof house of the children's own design.
Story stones or puppets of the three pigs and the wolf for retelling in the book corner.
A 'sorry wolf' ending on offer — soup, a party, a new friend — for children who want kindness to win.
Big-block building outdoors: houses children can actually climb inside and defend.

playing_exploring: Children throw themselves into the huffing, puffing, building and hiding — the story pulls them in bodily.
They test materials for real, blowing houses down again and again to see what happens.
active_learning: Children set out to build the strongest house and keep improving it until the wolf can't win.
They stick with a wobbly build, solving how to make it stand.
creating_thinking: Children predict which house will fall and reason about why bricks beat straw.
They rewrite the ending — a sorry wolf, a shared house — holding their own idea in mind.
